entries.contrast: North American covers Canada, the United States and Mexico. American on its own usually means only the United States.

entries.meaning: Of or from North Korea or its people. ---
examples: The North Korean delegation arrived on Tuesday.
He studies North Korean politics.
The defector is North Korean by birth.
entries.position: both — North Korean television, He is North Korean

entries.meaning: Traveling toward the north. ---
examples: The northbound lanes are backed up for miles.
We caught the northbound train at noon.
Most of the morning traffic is northbound.
entries.position: both

entries.meaning: On, in or facing the northeast. ---
examples: The storm came in over the northeast corner of the lake.
There's a service door on the northeast side.
A northeast wind picked up after dark.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: the northeast corner
entries.contrast: Also an adverb (head northeast) and a noun (the Northeast). For a region and its people use northeastern.

entries.meaning: Of or in the northeastern part of a country or region. ---
examples: She grew up in northeastern Ohio.
The northeastern states got two feet of snow.
It's a northeastern species of oak.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: northeastern states

entries.meaning: Northerly has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A northerly breeze cooled things off by evening.
The wind turned northerly overnight.
They set a northerly course out of the harbor.
We took the more northerly of the two routes.

senses.head: Of a wind: coming from the north
examples: A northerly breeze cooled things off by evening.
The wind turned northerly overnight.

senses.head: Lying toward or moving toward the north
examples: They set a northerly course out of the harbor.
We took the more northerly of the two routes.

entries.position: both
entries.form: -ly from north — an adjective, not an adverb
entries.contrast: Two traps. It ends in -ly but it is an adjective, so never "northerly-ly". And a northerly wind blows FROM the north, while a northerly course heads TOWARD it.

entries.meaning: Farthest to the north. ---
examples: Utqiagvik is the northernmost town in the United States.
The northernmost point of the island is a bare cliff.
We camped at the northernmost site in the park.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: the northernmost town

entries.meaning: On, in or facing the northwest. ---
examples: The northwest corner of the lot is still empty.
A northwest wind brought rain by morning.
Use the northwest stairwell during construction.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: the northwest corner
entries.contrast: Also an adverb (drive northwest) and a noun (the Pacific Northwest). For a region use northwestern.

entries.meaning: Of or in the northwestern part of a country or region. ---
examples: He teaches at a college in northwestern Montana.
Northwestern forests are full of Douglas fir.
It's a northwestern dialect you rarely hear back east.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: northwestern forests

entries.meaning: Nostalgic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He gets nostalgic about college every fall.
I'm nostalgic for the old neighborhood.
The show has a nostalgic 1980s soundtrack.
There's something nostalgic about the smell of chalk.

senses.head: Feeling a warm sadness about a time in the past
examples: He gets nostalgic about college every fall.
I'm nostalgic for the old neighborhood.

senses.head: Of a thing: bringing that feeling back
examples: The show has a nostalgic 1980s soundtrack.
There's something nostalgic about the smell of chalk.

entries.position: both
entries.contrast: Russian ностальгия often means missing home; English nostalgic is about missing a time, not a place. For missing home say homesick.

entries.meaning: Too interested in other people's private business. ---
examples: Our nosy neighbor watches everyone's mail.
Don't be nosy — it's none of your business.
The older she gets, the nosier she gets.
entries.русский: любопытный, сующий нос не в своё дело
entries.position: both
entries.form: -y from nose — sticking your nose in
entries.contrast: American spelling is nosy; nosey is a British variant. Note it is always a complaint — for harmless interest say curious.

entries.meaning: Notable has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The most notable change is the new roof.
The town is notable for its covered bridge.
Several notable writers signed the letter.
She's a notable figure in her field.

senses.head: Important or interesting enough to be worth mentioning
examples: The most notable change is the new roof.
The town is notable for its covered bridge.

senses.head: Of a person: well known and respected
examples: Several notable writers signed the letter.
She's a notable figure in her field.

entries.position: both
entries.form: -able from note, to take notice of
entries.contrast: Notable means worth noticing; noticeable means big enough to be seen or heard. A noticeable stain, a notable achievement.

entries.meaning: Having a small V-shaped cut or cuts in the edge. ---
examples: The blade has a notched edge for cutting rope.
He wore a jacket with notched lapels.
The stick was notched every few inches.
entries.position: both
entries.form: -ed from the noun notch, a small cut

entries.meaning: Well known, especially for one particular thing. ---
examples: A noted historian gave the keynote address.
The valley is noted for its apples.
She's a noted authority on wetlands.
entries.position: both — before a noun (a noted surgeon), or after a verb with for
entries.contrast: Before a noun, noted means famous. After a verb on its own it is just the past of note: Your objection is noted means it was written down, not that it is famous.

entries.meaning: Worth paying attention to. ---
examples: The noteworthy part is how fast they fixed it.
Nothing noteworthy happened all week.
Her essay makes several noteworthy points.
entries.position: both

entries.meaning: Easy to see, hear or feel. ---
examples: There's a noticeable dent in the door.
The difference is more noticeable in person.
His accent is barely noticeable now.
entries.position: both
entries.contrast: Keep the e in the middle: noticeable, never "noticable" — the e is what keeps the c soft.

entries.meaning: Well known for something bad. ---
examples: He's notorious for showing up late.
The prison held some of the country's most notorious criminals.
That stretch of highway is notorious.
entries.position: both
entries.contrast: Notorious is famous for something bad. A great scientist is famous, never notorious. Say a notorious intersection only if it is known for crashes.

entries.meaning: Full of what the body needs to stay healthy. ---
examples: A bowl of lentil soup is cheap and nourishing.
She made a nourishing stew that lasted all week.
Oatmeal is more nourishing than a donut.
entries.position: both
entries.form: -ing — what the food does for you

entries.meaning: New in a way nobody has tried before. ---
examples: She came up with a novel way to pay for it.
The idea was novel at the time.
It's a novel approach to a very old problem.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun
entries.contrast: A double false friend. The noun novel is a роман, a long book — and Russian новелла is a short story, not a novel at all. The adjective has nothing to do with books: it means new and original.

entries.meaning: Harmful or unpleasant to breathe, touch or live with. ---
examples: Noxious fumes drove everyone out of the building.
The state lists the plant as a noxious weed.
The smell coming from the drain was noxious.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun
entries.contrast: Noxious is harmful or foul-smelling — noxious fumes. Obnoxious is about a person being unbearable — an obnoxious guest. They are not related in meaning.

entries.meaning: Nuclear has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The country agreed to shut down its nuclear weapons program.
About a fifth of US electricity comes from nuclear plants.
Talks on nuclear disarmament resumed in Geneva.
She grew up in a traditional nuclear family of four.
The dye stains the nuclear membrane of each cell.

senses.head: Using the energy released by splitting atoms; involving atomic weapons
examples: The country agreed to shut down its nuclear weapons program.
About a fifth of US electricity comes from nuclear plants.
Talks on nuclear disarmament resumed in Geneva.

senses.head: Of the central core — of a cell, or of a family of parents and children
examples: She grew up in a traditional nuclear family of four.
The dye stains the nuclear membrane of each cell.

entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: nuclear power; after a verb: the plant is nuclear
entries.contrast: Say NOO-klee-ur. The common American mispronunciation NOO-kyuh-lur is heard from presidents and still counts as an error.

entries.meaning: Nude has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The class was drawing from a nude model.
Several of the statues are completely nude.
She wore nude heels with the black dress.
Nude lipstick is back in style.

senses.head: Wearing no clothes
examples: The class was drawing from a nude model.
Several of the statues are completely nude.

senses.head: Of a pale pinkish-beige color close to skin
examples: She wore nude heels with the black dress.
Nude lipstick is back in style.

entries.position: both — a nude model; the figures in the painting are nude
entries.contrast: Also a noun in art (a Modigliani nude) and in the phrase in the nude.

entries.meaning: Null has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The judge declared the contract null and void.
If you miss the deadline, the whole agreement becomes null.
The experiment produced a null result.
Statisticians start from the null hypothesis.

senses.head: Having no legal force
examples: The judge declared the contract null and void.
If you miss the deadline, the whole agreement becomes null.

senses.head: Equal to zero, or showing no effect
examples: The experiment produced a null result.
Statisticians start from the null hypothesis.

entries.position: both — a null result; in law almost always in the pair null and void
entries.contrast: In everyday English it lives inside the fixed phrase null and void. In programming null is a noun for an empty value.

entries.meaning: Numb has 2 distinct senses.
examples: My fingers were numb with cold.
The dentist waited until my jaw was completely numb.
She felt numb for weeks after the funeral.
The news left all of us numb.

senses.head: Unable to feel anything in part of the body
examples: My fingers were numb with cold.
The dentist waited until my jaw was completely numb.

senses.head: Unable to feel emotion, usually after a shock
examples: She felt numb for weeks after the funeral.
The news left all of us numb.

entries.position: both — numb fingers; my lips went numb
entries.contrast: The b is silent: NUM. The forms number and numbest exist, but Americans avoid them because number reads as the noun — say more numb.

entries.meaning: Numbing has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A numbing wind came off the lake.
The dentist applied a numbing gel first.
The job was a numbing routine of forms and phone calls.
There is something numbing about the constant bad news.

senses.head: Making the body lose feeling
examples: A numbing wind came off the lake.
The dentist applied a numbing gel first.

senses.head: So dull or so repeated that it deadens the mind
examples: The job was a numbing routine of forms and phone calls.
There is something numbing about the constant bad news.

entries.position: both — a numbing cold; the routine was numbing

entries.meaning: Expressed in numbers; made of digits. ---
examples: The password has to contain at least one numeric character.
Use the numeric keypad on the right side of the keyboard.
That column accepts numeric values only.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: a numeric code; the field must be numeric
entries.contrast: numeric and numerical mean the same thing. Computing prefers numeric (a numeric keypad); order and analysis prefer numerical (numerical order).

entries.meaning: Relating to numbers, or measured by them. ---
examples: Please file the folders in numerical order.
The army had a clear numerical advantage.
We ran a numerical analysis of the survey answers.
entries.position: both — numerical order; the advantage was purely numerical
entries.contrast: See numeric. The adverb numerically is common in writing: numerically superior.

entries.meaning: Existing in large numbers; many. ---
examples: We received numerous complaints about the noise.
She has made numerous attempts to reach him.
Deer are far more numerous here than they were twenty years ago.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: numerous complaints; her awards are too numerous to list
entries.contrast: numerous counts things, so it needs a plural countable noun: numerous problems, never numerous money.

entries.meaning: Relating to nutrition and to the food value of what people eat. ---
examples: The label lists the nutritional information for one serving.
Processing strips much of the nutritional value out of the grain.
She has a degree in nutritional science.
entries.position: attributive only — nutritional value; not the meal is nutritional
entries.contrast: nutritional is about nutrition as a subject (nutritional information); food that is good for you is nutritious. A meal is nutritious, never nutritional.

entries.meaning: Containing what the body needs; good for you. ---
examples: Oatmeal makes a cheap, nutritious breakfast.
Fresh vegetables are more nutritious than canned ones.
The district is trying to serve nutritious school lunches.
entries.position: both — a nutritious breakfast; the soup is cheap and nutritious
entries.contrast: See nutritional. nutritious praises the food itself.

entries.meaning: Nuts has 2 distinct senses.
examples: You'd be nuts to turn down that offer.
The noise from upstairs is driving me nuts.
My daughter is nuts about horses.
He's absolutely nuts for that band.

senses.head: Crazy; not thinking sensibly
examples: You'd be nuts to turn down that offer.
The noise from upstairs is driving me nuts.

senses.head: Extremely enthusiastic about something
examples: My daughter is nuts about horses.
He's absolutely nuts for that band.

entries.position: predicative only — he's nuts; never a nuts idea
entries.contrast: Informal. Before a noun you must switch words: a crazy idea, not a nuts idea. The noun nuts (орехи) is a different word altogether.

entries.meaning: Nutty has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The bread has a warm, nutty flavor.
This coffee is nuttier than the one we had yesterday.
He has some nutty ideas about money.
Her nutty uncle shows up every Thanksgiving.

senses.head: Tasting or smelling of nuts
examples: The bread has a warm, nutty flavor.
This coffee is nuttier than the one we had yesterday.

senses.head: Slightly crazy — informal and usually affectionate
examples: He has some nutty ideas about money.
Her nutty uncle shows up every Thanksgiving.

entries.position: both — a nutty flavor; the cheese tastes nutty

entries.meaning: Behaving like a clumsy, rude, stupid man. ---
examples: His oafish jokes made everyone at the table uncomfortable.
She apologized for her brother's oafish behavior.
The character is written as a big, oafish bully.
entries.position: both — oafish behavior; he was loud and oafish
entries.form: -ish from oaf, a clumsy stupid man

entries.meaning: Doing what you are told to do. ---
examples: They trained the puppy to be obedient.
He was a quiet, obedient student who never caused trouble.
Soldiers are expected to be obedient to orders.
entries.position: both — an obedient dog; the children were obedient
entries.takes: to + noun: obedient to the law

entries.meaning: So overweight that health is at risk. ---
examples: The doctor told him he was clinically obese.
The program helps obese children get more exercise.
The share of obese adults has risen sharply since the 1980s.
entries.position: both — obese patients; he was clinically obese
entries.contrast: A medical word. Said of a person you know it sounds blunt or cruel — overweight is the everyday word.

entries.meaning: Likely to offend people or make them protest. ---
examples: Several parents found the book objectionable.
The site removes objectionable content within a day.
He said nothing objectionable, but the tone was all wrong.
entries.position: both — objectionable content; the ad was objectionable

entries.meaning: Objective has 2 distinct senses.
examples: It's hard to be objective about your own children.
We need an objective review from someone outside the team.
There is no objective evidence that the drug works.
The test gives an objective measure of reading level.

senses.head: Not influenced by personal feelings; fair
examples: It's hard to be objective about your own children.
We need an objective review from someone outside the team.

senses.head: Based on facts that exist independently of anyone's opinion
examples: There is no objective evidence that the drug works.
The test gives an objective measure of reading level.

entries.position: both — an objective report; try to stay objective
entries.contrast: objective is also a noun meaning a goal: our main objective this quarter. Same spelling, different word class.

entries.meaning: Having a legal or moral duty to do something. ---
examples: You are not obligated to say anything without a lawyer.
I felt obligated to invite her.
The company is legally obligated to notify customers.
entries.position: predicative only — you're not obligated to answer; never an obligated guest
entries.contrast: obligated is the American form for a duty you actually have. obliged covers the same ground and adds the sense 'grateful'. Neither one goes before a noun.

entries.meaning: Required by a rule or by custom. ---
examples: A first-aid class is obligatory for all new staff.
Attendance at the Monday meeting is obligatory.
He posted the obligatory photo of his feet on the beach.
entries.position: both — an obligatory course; attendance is obligatory
entries.contrast: Often used jokingly for the thing everybody always does: the obligatory family photo.

entries.meaning: Obliged has 2 distinct senses.
examples: I felt obliged to say something.
Banks are obliged to report large transfers.
I'd be much obliged if you'd take a look at this.
Much obliged, ma'am.

senses.head: Having a duty to do something
examples: I felt obliged to say something.
Banks are obliged to report large transfers.

senses.head: Grateful to someone
examples: I'd be much obliged if you'd take a look at this.
Much obliged, ma'am.

entries.position: predicative only — I felt obliged to help; never an obliged friend
entries.takes: to-infinitive; to + person (in the grateful sense)
entries.contrast: See obligated. Much obliged is a slightly old-fashioned, rural-sounding American 'thank you'.

entries.meaning: Willing and eager to help. ---
examples: The hotel staff were friendly and obliging.
An obliging stranger helped us carry the suitcase up.
She is always obliging when you ask for a favor.
entries.position: both — an obliging neighbor; the staff were very obliging
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with obliged (обязанный). obliging describes someone glad to help.

entries.meaning: Oblique has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She made an oblique reference to his drinking.
The answer was so oblique that nobody understood it.
The light came in at an oblique angle.
Cut the stem at an oblique angle before putting it in water.

senses.head: Not said directly; only hinted at
examples: She made an oblique reference to his drinking.
The answer was so oblique that nobody understood it.

senses.head: Sloping; at an angle that is not a right angle
examples: The light came in at an oblique angle.
Cut the stem at an oblique angle before putting it in water.

entries.position: both — an oblique reference; his answer was oblique

entries.meaning: Not noticing what is happening around you. ---
examples: He walked on, oblivious to the traffic around him.
She seemed completely oblivious of the effect she had on people.
The kids kept playing, oblivious to the rain.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: he was oblivious to the noise; also an oblivious driver
entries.contrast: It does not mean 'forgetful'. oblivious to means failing to notice something that is right in front of you.

entries.meaning: Longer than it is wide, with straight sides. ---
examples: They served the cake on an oblong platter.
The garden is a narrow oblong strip behind the house.
Trace an oblong shape on the cardboard and cut it out.
entries.position: both — an oblong table; the room is long and oblong
entries.contrast: In American use it means longer than it is wide — normally a rectangle. It is also a noun: cut the dough into oblongs.

entries.meaning: Extremely unpleasant, usually in a loud and rude way. ---
examples: The guy behind us was loud and obnoxious the whole game.
He gets obnoxious after two beers.
That is the most obnoxious ad on television.
entries.position: both — an obnoxious guy; the music was obnoxious
entries.contrast: One of the most common American insults for someone loud and rude. Stronger than annoying, and about behavior rather than looks.

entries.meaning: Obscene has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He was arrested for shouting obscene remarks at passersby.
The station was fined for broadcasting obscene material.
They pay their executives obscene bonuses.
The price of a two-bedroom here is obscene.

senses.head: Offensive in a sexual way; indecent
examples: He was arrested for shouting obscene remarks at passersby.
The station was fined for broadcasting obscene material.

senses.head: So extreme that it is morally shocking — usually about money
examples: They pay their executives obscene bonuses.
The price of a two-bedroom here is obscene.

entries.position: both — obscene language; the joke was obscene

entries.meaning: Obscure has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He collects records by obscure jazz musicians.
She quoted some obscure nineteenth-century poet.
For reasons that remain obscure, the project was canceled.
The instructions were written in the most obscure language imaginable.

senses.head: Known by very few people
examples: He collects records by obscure jazz musicians.
She quoted some obscure nineteenth-century poet.

senses.head: Hard to understand or see clearly
examples: For reasons that remain obscure, the project was canceled.
The instructions were written in the most obscure language imaginable.

entries.position: both — an obscure poet; the reason remains obscure
entries.contrast: Also a verb with the same stress: Clouds obscured the moon.

entries.meaning: Trying too hard to please someone important. ---
examples: The waiter's obsequious manner made the whole meal uncomfortable.
He is obsequious to anyone with money.
She could not stand his obsequious emails to the director.
entries.position: both — an obsequious waiter; he was obsequious to the boss
entries.contrast: Always negative — flattery too eager to be sincere. Formal; in speech Americans say fawning or the blunt kiss-up.

entries.meaning: Able to be seen or measured. ---
examples: There was no observable difference between the two groups.
The drug produced an observable drop in blood pressure.
Science works with what is observable and measurable.
entries.position: both — an observable change; the effect is easily observable
entries.contrast: observable is what can be seen; observant is the person doing the seeing.

entries.meaning: Observant has 2 distinct senses.
examples: A good nurse has to be observant.
She is more observant than anyone else in the family.
They come from an observant Jewish family.
He became observant in his thirties.

senses.head: Quick to notice things
examples: A good nurse has to be observant.
She is more observant than anyone else in the family.

senses.head: Careful to follow the rules and holidays of a religion
examples: They come from an observant Jewish family.
He became observant in his thirties.

entries.position: both — an observant child; she is very observant
entries.contrast: See observable.

entries.meaning: Based on watching rather than on experiment. ---
examples: The findings come from an observational study of 4,000 nurses.
Most of the evidence is observational, not experimental.
He does observational comedy about everyday life.
entries.position: both — an observational study; the evidence is purely observational
entries.contrast: A research word: an observational study only watches, while an experiment changes something. Not the same as observant.

entries.meaning: Thinking about one thing far too much, in a way you cannot control. ---
examples: She is obsessive about keeping the kitchen clean.
The film shows his obsessive need to win.
Checking your phone every minute is obsessive.
entries.position: both — obsessive behavior; he's obsessive about his car

entries.meaning: Having unwanted repeated thoughts and the rituals people use to quiet them. ---
examples: He was diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder at fifteen.
Therapy helped her manage the obsessive-compulsive rituals.
The clinic specializes in obsessive-compulsive and anxiety disorders.
entries.position: both — obsessive-compulsive disorder; the behavior is obsessive-compulsive
entries.form: compound — two adjectives joined by a hyphen
entries.contrast: A clinical term, nearly always in the full name obsessive-compulsive disorder, shortened to OCD. Calling a tidy friend 'so OCD' is casual slang, not a diagnosis.

entries.meaning: No longer used, because something better has replaced it. ---
examples: Fax machines are almost obsolete in most offices.
The company still runs on obsolete software.
New technology made the whole job obsolete.
entries.position: both — obsolete equipment; the format is obsolete
entries.contrast: obsolete means no longer used at all. Something merely old-fashioned is outdated.

entries.meaning: Refusing to change your mind, however good the arguments are. ---
examples: He was obstinate and refused to see a doctor.
The talks failed because both sides were obstinate.
It is an obstinate stain that will not come out of the carpet.
entries.position: both — an obstinate child; he was obstinate about it
entries.contrast: Negative, like stubborn but more formal. The approving word for the same quality is determined.

entries.meaning: Noisy and difficult to control. ---
examples: Security removed an obstreperous fan from the stands.
The class gets obstreperous on the last day before vacation.
He was a loud, obstreperous guest at every party.
entries.position: both — an obstreperous crowd; the kids got obstreperous
entries.contrast: Formal and often half-joking. In plain speech Americans say rowdy or unruly.

entries.meaning: Obstructive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The committee accused the agency of being obstructive.
He was charged with obstructive conduct during the search.
She was treated for obstructive sleep apnea.
Obstructive lung disease makes breathing out difficult.

senses.head: Deliberately getting in the way of something
examples: The committee accused the agency of being obstructive.
He was charged with obstructive conduct during the search.

senses.head: Blocking a passage in the body — a medical use
examples: She was treated for obstructive sleep apnea.
Obstructive lung disease makes breathing out difficult.

entries.position: both — obstructive tactics; the agency was obstructive

entries.meaning: Able to be got, if you go to the right place. ---
examples: The forms are obtainable from any post office.
The chemical is easily obtainable online.
Tickets are obtainable only through the box office.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: the permit is obtainable online; also an easily obtainable drug

entries.meaning: Noticeable in an unwelcome way. ---
examples: The security cameras are large and obtrusive.
He tried to take photos without being obtrusive.
The new building is more obtrusive than the old one.
entries.position: both — an obtrusive camera; the ads are obtrusive
entries.contrast: The negative unobtrusive is the more common of the pair: an unobtrusive waiter.

entries.meaning: Obtuse has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Stop being deliberately obtuse.
He is not stupid, just obtuse when it suits him.
An obtuse angle is wider than a right angle.
Draw a triangle with one obtuse angle.

senses.head: Slow to understand — often said when you suspect the person is pretending
examples: Stop being deliberately obtuse.
He is not stupid, just obtuse when it suits him.

senses.head: Of an angle: between 90 and 180 degrees
examples: An obtuse angle is wider than a right angle.
Draw a triangle with one obtuse angle.

entries.position: both — an obtuse angle; don't be obtuse

entries.meaning: Happening from time to time, not often or regularly. ---
examples: She still has an occasional cigarette.
We get the occasional complaint, but nothing serious.
The forecast is sun with occasional showers.
entries.position: attributive only — an occasional cigarette; not the cigarettes are occasional
entries.contrast: It means 'now and then', not 'по случаю'. Learners more often need the adverb: I occasionally drink coffee.

entries.meaning: Relating to magic and hidden supernatural forces. ---
examples: The library has a shelf of books on occult practices.
He got interested in occult symbols as a teenager.
The movie mixes horror with occult ritual.
entries.position: attributive only — occult practices; after a verb English uses the noun phrase the occult
entries.contrast: You will usually meet it as a noun: an interest in the occult. Some Americans stress the first syllable: AH-kult.

entries.meaning: Relating to a job and to the risks and training that go with it. ---
examples: Back pain is an occupational hazard for nurses.
She works as an occupational therapist.
The agency sets occupational safety standards.
entries.position: attributive only — occupational therapy; not the risk was occupational
entries.contrast: It means 'to do with your job', not 'skilled'. An occupational hazard is a risk that comes with the work.

entries.meaning: Occupied has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Every table in the place was occupied.
The sign on the restroom door said occupied.
The puzzle kept the kids occupied for an hour.
She is fully occupied with the new baby.
They grew up in occupied territory.
Life in the occupied zone was tightly controlled.

senses.head: In use, so not free
examples: Every table in the place was occupied.
The sign on the restroom door said occupied.

senses.head: Busy with something
examples: The puzzle kept the kids occupied for an hour.
She is fully occupied with the new baby.

senses.head: Held by a foreign army
examples: They grew up in occupied territory.
Life in the occupied zone was tightly controlled.

entries.position: both — occupied territory; all the seats are occupied

entries.meaning: Belonging to or coming from the ocean. ---
examples: Oceanic currents move heat around the planet.
The islands have a mild oceanic climate.
She studies oceanic food chains.
entries.position: both — mostly before a noun: oceanic currents; the climate here is oceanic

entries.meaning: Of a brownish-yellow color, like the earth pigment. ---
examples: They painted the kitchen an ocher yellow.
The cave walls are covered in ocher handprints.
She wore an ocher scarf with a gray coat.
entries.position: both — ocher walls; the cliffs are ocher
entries.contrast: American spelling ocher; British writing has ochre. It is also a noun for the earth pigment itself.

entries.meaning: Having eight straight sides. ---
examples: American stop signs are octagonal.
The gazebo has an octagonal roof.
They bought an octagonal mirror for the hallway.
entries.position: both — an octagonal table; the tower is octagonal

entries.meaning: Between eighty and eighty-nine years old. ---
examples: The team is coached by an octogenarian legend.
Two octogenarian senators are running again.
The paper ran a story about an octogenarian marathon runner.
entries.position: attributive only — an octogenarian senator; after a verb English uses the noun
entries.contrast: Much more common as a noun: a lively octogenarian. Formal or journalistic either way.

entries.meaning: Most likely to win or to happen. ---
examples: She is the odds-on favorite to win the nomination.
The odds-on choice lost in the first round.
He went in as the odds-on favorite and left with nothing.
entries.position: attributive only — the odds-on favorite; American English avoids he is odds-on
entries.contrast: Almost always in the fixed phrase the odds-on favorite.

entries.meaning: Deserving hatred; extremely unpleasant. ---
examples: The law was called odious by every human rights group.
He made an odious comparison between the two events.
It is an odious job, but somebody has to do it.
entries.position: both — an odious comparison; the practice is odious
entries.contrast: Formal and strong. Nothing to do with smell — the adjective from odor is odorous.

entries.meaning: Having no smell. ---
examples: Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless.
They make an odorless version of the paint.
The powder is completely odorless.
entries.position: both — an odorless gas; the cleaner is odorless
entries.contrast: American spelling odorless; British odourless.

entries.meaning: Off has 3 distinct senses.
examples: Make sure the stove is off before you leave.
All the lights were off when we got home.
The wedding is off.
If it rains, the game is off.
The pitcher was having an off day.
Something about his story felt off.

senses.head: Not working; switched off
examples: Make sure the stove is off before you leave.
All the lights were off when we got home.

senses.head: Canceled; not happening after all
examples: The wedding is off.
If it rains, the game is off.

senses.head: Below the usual standard; not quite right
examples: The pitcher was having an off day.
Something about his story felt off.

entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: the lights are off; before a noun only in fixed uses: an off day, the off season
entries.contrast: off is far more often a preposition or an adverb (take it off the shelf, he drove off). It counts as an adjective when it follows be or sits in an off day.

entries.meaning: Not ready for what happens. ---
examples: The question caught me completely off guard.
The announcement took the whole staff off guard.
He was off guard for a second, and that was enough.
entries.position: predicative only — the question caught me off guard; never before a noun
entries.contrast: Nearly always after catch or take. Before a noun English switches words: an unprepared witness, not an off guard witness.

entries.meaning: Off the hook has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The check cleared, so you are off the hook.
Her confession let the other two off the hook.
He left the phone off the hook all weekend.
The line was busy because the receiver was off the hook.

senses.head: No longer in trouble, or no longer responsible for something
examples: The check cleared, so you are off the hook.
Her confession let the other two off the hook.

senses.head: Of a telephone: not hung up
examples: He left the phone off the hook all weekend.
The line was busy because the receiver was off the hook.

entries.position: predicative only — you're off the hook; never before a noun
entries.contrast: An idiom. The literal sense is a telephone receiver left off its cradle, which is where the figure of speech came from.

entries.meaning: Completely wrong in what you think or say. ---
examples: Your estimate is way off-base.
He apologized and admitted his comment was off-base.
That is an off-base reading of what she actually said.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: that's way off-base; also an off-base comparison
entries.form: compound — from baseball, a runner caught off base
entries.contrast: American, from baseball, and usually strengthened by way: way off-base.

entries.meaning: Off-center has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The picture hangs a little off-center.
An off-center part makes the whole wheel wobble.
The show has a nice off-center sense of humor.
He plays the off-center neighbor in the sitcom.

senses.head: Not exactly in the middle
examples: The picture hangs a little off-center.
An off-center part makes the whole wheel wobble.

senses.head: A bit odd or unconventional
examples: The show has a nice off-center sense of humor.
He plays the off-center neighbor in the sitcom.

entries.position: both — an off-center design; the photo is slightly off-center
entries.contrast: American spelling off-center; British off-centre.

entries.meaning: Mildly indecent, especially of a joke. ---
examples: He told an off-color joke at the reception.
The comedy special gets off-color fast.
Keep the toasts short and nothing off-color.
entries.position: both — an off-color joke; the humor got off-color
entries.contrast: American spelling off-color. In the US it means mildly indecent. British off colour can mean 'unwell', a sense American English does not have.

entries.meaning: Off-key has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The whole second verse was off-key.
He hit an off-key note and laughed.
His cheerful speech felt off-key that day.
The ad campaign struck an off-key note.

senses.head: Not on the right musical note
examples: The whole second verse was off-key.
He hit an off-key note and laughed.

senses.head: Striking the wrong tone for the occasion
examples: His cheerful speech felt off-key that day.
The ad campaign struck an off-key note.

entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: the second verse was off-key; also an off-key note
entries.contrast: Also a very common adverb: She sang off-key.

entries.meaning: Not allowed to be entered, used or discussed. ---
examples: The basement is off-limits to guests.
That topic is off-limits at dinner.
The beach is off-limits after dark.
entries.position: predicative only — the roof is off-limits; never before a noun
entries.form: compound — originally the wording on a US military sign

entries.meaning: Not connected to a network, or not currently running. ---
examples: The whole system was off-line for six hours.
Keep a copy in off-line storage.
She keeps her off-line life private.
entries.position: both — off-line storage; the server is off-line
entries.contrast: Now usually written offline, without the hyphen. Also an adverb, and in offices take this offline means 'discuss it privately later'.

entries.meaning: Unpleasant enough to make you want to keep away. ---
examples: The smell in the hallway was off-putting.
His first email was a little off-putting.
Some people find her directness off-putting.
entries.position: both — an off-putting smell; his manner was off-putting
entries.form: compound — from the phrasal verb put off, 'оттолкнуть'

entries.meaning: Away from the main building or location. ---
examples: The hotel offers off-site parking for ten dollars a day.
Backups are kept in an off-site facility.
Next week's meeting is off-site.
entries.position: both — off-site parking; the training is off-site
entries.contrast: Also an adverb (the data is stored off-site) and, in business, a noun: a two-day off-site.

entries.meaning: In a driveway or lot rather than on the public street. ---
examples: The apartment comes with off-street parking.
Off-street spaces rent for an extra hundred a month.
The listing mentions two off-street spots.
entries.position: attributive only — off-street parking; not the parking is off-street
entries.contrast: You will meet it almost only in apartment listings, in the phrase off-street parking — a driveway or lot instead of the curb.

entries.meaning: Said without preparation. ---
examples: It was an off-the-cuff remark that got him in trouble.
Her answers were off-the-cuff but sharp.
He gave an off-the-cuff toast at the rehearsal dinner.
entries.position: both — an off-the-cuff remark; his answer was off-the-cuff
entries.form: compound — as if reading notes scribbled on a shirt cuff
entries.contrast: After a verb it is often written without hyphens, as an adverb: He spoke off the cuff.

entries.meaning: Bought ready-made in a standard size, not made to measure. ---
examples: He wore an off-the-rack suit to the interview.
Off-the-rack sizes never fit him right.
The dress looks expensive, but it is off-the-rack.
entries.position: both — an off-the-rack suit; the jacket is off-the-rack
entries.contrast: The American phrase for ready-made clothes; the British say off the peg. For software and parts the phrase is off-the-shelf.

entries.meaning: Ready-made and available to buy, rather than built to order. ---
examples: They built the site with off-the-shelf software.
Off-the-shelf parts are much cheaper than custom ones.
Most of the hardware is off-the-shelf.
entries.position: both — off-the-shelf software; the parts are off-the-shelf
entries.contrast: About products, especially software and parts. For clothes the phrase is off-the-rack.

entries.meaning: Cut to leave the shoulders bare. ---
examples: She wore an off-the-shoulder dress to the wedding.
Off-the-shoulder tops are back in style.
The neckline is off-the-shoulder.
entries.position: both — an off-the-shoulder dress; the neckline is off-the-shoulder

entries.meaning: Very unusual or eccentric. ---
examples: He came up with an off-the-wall idea that actually worked.
Her sense of humor is completely off-the-wall.
The show is the most off-the-wall thing on television.
entries.position: both — an off-the-wall idea; his humor is off-the-wall
entries.contrast: Informal and usually friendly: strange in an original way, not disturbing.

entries.meaning: White with a faint tint of gray, yellow or cream. ---
examples: We painted the living room off-white.
She chose an off-white dress instead of pure white.
The old pages have turned a dingy off-white.
entries.русский: не чисто белый, белый с оттенком
entries.position: both — off-white walls; the paint is off-white

entries.meaning: Unusual and a little quirky, in a likable way. ---
examples: It is an offbeat comedy about a family of undertakers.
The town has an offbeat charm.
She has an offbeat way of telling a story.
entries.position: both — an offbeat comedy; the style is offbeat
entries.form: compound — from music, a beat that falls off the main pulse
entries.contrast: Usually a compliment: unusual in an interesting way. off-the-wall is the stronger word.

entries.meaning: Hurt or angry because of something rude. ---
examples: She was offended by his tone.
Several viewers wrote in, offended that the network aired it.
An offended customer posted the whole exchange online.
entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: she was offended; also an offended customer
entries.contrast: offended is what the person feels; offensive is what the thing is: I was offended by the offensive joke.

entries.meaning: Offensive has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The ad was pulled after viewers called it offensive.
He apologized for the offensive language.
They traded for help on the offensive line.
The treaty bans offensive weapons.

senses.head: Rude or insulting; causing anger
examples: The ad was pulled after viewers called it offensive.
He apologized for the offensive language.

senses.head: Used for attacking rather than defending
examples: They traded for help on the offensive line.
The treaty bans offensive weapons.

entries.position: both — an offensive remark; the joke was offensive
entries.contrast: See offended. In sports and the military the stress moves to the front: the AWF-en-siv line.

entries.meaning: Said casually, without much thought or care. ---
examples: It was an offhand comment, but it stuck with me.
She was oddly offhand about the whole diagnosis.
He gave an offhand answer and changed the subject.
entries.position: both — an offhand comment; he was offhand about it
entries.contrast: Also a very common adverb meaning 'without checking': I don't know offhand. The adjective means casual, sometimes rudely so.

entries.meaning: Casual to the point of seeming not to care. ---
examples: He made an offhanded remark about her weight.
Her tone was offhanded, almost bored.
The apology felt offhanded.
entries.position: both — an offhanded remark; his tone was offhanded
entries.contrast: The same meaning as offhand, and the adverb from it, offhandedly, is the one Americans reach for most.

entries.meaning: Official has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Spanish is an official language in twenty countries.
The results will not be official until Friday.
She was there in an official capacity.
He used the official car for personal trips.

senses.head: Approved by a government or organization; formally announced
examples: Spanish is an official language in twenty countries.
The results will not be official until Friday.

senses.head: Connected with a job or a position of authority
examples: She was there in an official capacity.
He used the official car for personal trips.

entries.position: both — the official language; the results are official
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a city official (должностное лицо). Do not confuse it with officious, which means bossy.

entries.meaning: Too eager to use a small amount of authority. ---
examples: An officious clerk made us fill out the form three times.
The guard was officious about the parking rules.
He becomes officious the moment you hand him a clipboard.
entries.position: both — an officious clerk; the guard was officious
entries.contrast: A classic trap. officious is not official, and not Russian официозный. It describes a minor official who enjoys giving orders.

entries.meaning: Offshore has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The state approved two offshore wind farms.
Offshore drilling has been banned along that coast.
The money sat in an offshore account for years.
They moved the whole support team offshore.

senses.head: In the sea, at a distance from the coast
examples: The state approved two offshore wind farms.
Offshore drilling has been banned along that coast.

senses.head: Placed in another country, usually to pay less tax
examples: The money sat in an offshore account for years.
They moved the whole support team offshore.

entries.position: both — offshore drilling; the accounts are offshore

entries.meaning: Oily has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He wiped his oily hands on a rag.
This fish is oilier than salmon.
The salesman had an oily charm.
There was something oily about his compliments.

senses.head: Covered in oil, or containing a lot of it
examples: He wiped his oily hands on a rag.
This fish is oilier than salmon.

senses.head: Too smooth and flattering to be trusted — of a person
examples: The salesman had an oily charm.
There was something oily about his compliments.

entries.position: both — oily skin; the sauce tastes oily

entries.meaning: Okay has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Are you okay? That was a hard fall.
The kids are okay, just shaken up.
The movie was okay, nothing special.
Is it okay if I bring a friend?

senses.head: Unhurt, healthy or safe
examples: Are you okay? That was a hard fall.
The kids are okay, just shaken up.

senses.head: Acceptable, but no better than that
examples: The movie was okay, nothing special.
Is it okay if I bring a friend?

entries.position: both — mostly after a verb: are you okay?; also an okay movie
entries.contrast: Also spelled OK. The same word works as an adjective (the food was okay), an adverb (she did okay), a noun (I need your okay) and a verb (the board okayed it).

entries.meaning: Belonging to or in the style of an earlier time. ---
examples: They play old-time fiddle music at the festival.
The diner has an old-time feel.
He believes in old-time religion.
entries.position: attributive only — old-time music; not the music is old-time
entries.contrast: Warm and nostalgic, never an insult. The related old-timer is a noun for a longtime member or an old man.

entries.meaning: Having the charm and courtesy associated with old Europe. ---
examples: The hotel has a certain old-world charm.
He greeted her with old-world courtesy.
The café is full of old-world details — brass, velvet and dark wood.
entries.position: attributive only — old-world charm; not the hotel is old-world
entries.form: compound — from the Old World, meaning Europe
entries.contrast: Usually a compliment about European-style charm and manners. Capitalized, the Old World is a noun for Europe, Asia and Africa.

entries.meaning: Relating to the sense of smell. ---
examples: The olfactory nerve carries signals from the nose to the brain.
The virus damaged her olfactory system.
Perfumers train their olfactory memory for years.
entries.position: attributive only — the olfactory nerve; not the sense is olfactory

entries.meaning: Of a dull yellowish-green color; of skin, warm light brown. ---
examples: He wore an olive jacket and jeans.
She has dark hair and olive skin.
The bedroom walls are a soft olive green.
entries.position: both — an olive jacket; the walls are olive
entries.contrast: As a color it is a dark yellow-green. But olive skin means a warm light-brown complexion, not a green one. The fruit olive is a noun.

entries.meaning: Calm and superior, as a god looking down on human affairs. ---
examples: She watched the argument with Olympian calm.
He wrote with an Olympian detachment from ordinary life.
The judges kept an Olympian distance from the press.
entries.position: both — Olympian calm; his detachment was Olympian
entries.form: from Olympus, the mountain of the Greek gods
entries.contrast: Also a noun for an athlete who competes in the Games: a three-time Olympian. The adjective for the Games themselves is Olympic.

entries.meaning: Relating to the Olympic Games. ---
examples: She won an Olympic gold medal in Tokyo.
The pool is Olympic size.
He trains with the Olympic team.
entries.position: attributive only — an Olympic medal; not the medal is Olympic
entries.form: from Olympia, where the ancient games were held
entries.contrast: Olympic is for the Games; Olympian is for the gods, or a noun for an athlete competing.

entries.meaning: From or relating to Oman. ---
examples: The Omani government signed the agreement.
We ate at an Omani restaurant in Dearborn.
Most of the crew were Omani.
entries.position: both — Omani oil; most of the crew were Omani
entries.contrast: Also a noun for a person from Oman: two Omanis. Nationality words are always capitalized in English.

entries.meaning: Suggesting that something bad is about to happen. ---
examples: There was an ominous silence on the other end of the line.
Dark, ominous clouds moved in from the west.
The last paragraph of the memo was ominous.
entries.position: both — an ominous silence; the sky looked ominous

entries.meaning: Covering many separate items in a single package. ---
examples: Congress passed an omnibus spending bill at the last minute.
The omnibus edition collects all three novels.
Lawmakers buried the change in an omnibus package.
entries.position: attributive only — an omnibus bill; not the bill is omnibus
entries.contrast: In American news this almost always means one large bill or book that packs many separate items together. The old sense 'bus' survives only in British English.

entries.meaning: Having unlimited power. ---
examples: They believe in an omnipotent and loving God.
The company acts as though it were omnipotent.
No government is omnipotent.
entries.position: both — an omnipotent god; the state is not omnipotent

entries.meaning: Present everywhere at once. ---
examples: Security cameras are omnipresent in the airport.
The omnipresent hum of traffic never stops.
Her phone is omnipresent, even at dinner.
entries.position: both — the omnipresent cameras; advertising is omnipresent

entries.meaning: Knowing everything. ---
examples: The novel is told by an omniscient narrator.
Nobody on the committee is omniscient.
The story shifts from first person to omniscient.
entries.position: both — an omniscient narrator; the narrator is omniscient
entries.contrast: Most Americans meet this word in the literature classroom: an omniscient narrator knows every character's thoughts.

entries.meaning: Eating both plants and meat. ---
examples: Bears are omnivorous — they eat berries and fish.
Humans are an omnivorous species.
She was an omnivorous reader, finishing three books a week.
entries.position: both — an omnivorous animal; bears are omnivorous
entries.contrast: Also used figuratively about appetites of the mind: an omnivorous reader.

entries.meaning: On has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The oven is on.
Leave the porch light on.
The concert is still on despite the rain.
Dinner at seven — are we still on?

senses.head: Working; switched on
examples: The oven is on.
Leave the porch light on.

senses.head: Happening as planned
examples: The concert is still on despite the rain.
Dinner at seven — are we still on?

entries.position: predicative only — the lights are on; the game is still on
entries.contrast: on is overwhelmingly a preposition (on the table) or an adverb (keep going on). It is an adjective only after be, meaning 'working' or 'happening as planned'.

entries.meaning: Located at the place where the work or activity happens. ---
examples: The building has an on-site gym and laundry.
There is an on-site manager for emergencies.
All of the training is on-site.
entries.position: both — on-site parking; the nurse is on-site
entries.contrast: Also an adverb: The engineer works on-site three days a week.

entries.meaning: Happening at work, while you are doing the work. ---
examples: The company provides two weeks of on-the-job training.
She filed a claim for an on-the-job injury.
Most of what he knows came from on-the-job experience.
entries.русский: без отрыва от производства, на рабочем месте
entries.position: attributive only — on-the-job training; not the training is on-the-job
entries.contrast: Almost always on-the-job training or an on-the-job injury. After a verb the hyphens drop: He was injured on the job.

entries.meaning: Done immediately, right where the situation is. ---
examples: Officers can issue an on-the-spot fine.
She was hired in an on-the-spot decision.
The network filed an on-the-spot report from the scene.
entries.position: attributive only — an on-the-spot fine; not the fine was on-the-spot
entries.contrast: Without hyphens it is an adverb phrase: They fined him on the spot. The idiom put someone on the spot means to force a hard answer.

entries.meaning: Moving toward you. ---
examples: He drifted into the oncoming lane.
Dim your headlights for oncoming traffic.
She stepped back from the oncoming crowd.
entries.position: attributive only — oncoming traffic; not the traffic was oncoming
entries.contrast: Above all a driving word: oncoming traffic is the traffic coming toward you.

entries.meaning: Having only one arm. ---
examples: The story is about a one-armed pitcher who made the majors.
He can do a one-armed pull-up.
Casinos used to be full of one-armed bandits.
entries.position: attributive only — a one-armed man; not the man is one-armed
entries.contrast: The pattern number + noun + -ed builds many adjectives: two-story, four-door, one-eyed. A slot machine is a one-armed bandit.

entries.meaning: One-dimensional has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The villain is one-dimensional and never becomes interesting.
His view of the city is one-dimensional.
A line is a one-dimensional object.
The model reduces the flow to a one-dimensional problem.

senses.head: Having no depth — of people, characters or arguments
examples: The villain is one-dimensional and never becomes interesting.
His view of the city is one-dimensional.

senses.head: Having only one dimension — in math and physics
examples: A line is a one-dimensional object.
The model reduces the flow to a one-dimensional problem.

entries.position: both — a one-dimensional character; the villain is one-dimensional

entries.meaning: Having only one eye. ---
examples: They adopted a one-eyed cat from the shelter.
He drew a one-eyed monster on the napkin.
In the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king.
entries.position: attributive only — a one-eyed cat; not the cat is one-eyed
entries.contrast: Built like one-armed. The proverb runs: in the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king.

entries.meaning: Done with or using only one hand. ---
examples: He made a one-handed catch at the fence.
There's a one-handed way to open the jar.
The drill is light enough for one-handed use.
entries.position: both
entries.contrast: The same word is also an adverb: He caught it one-handed. There it tells you how, not what kind.

entries.meaning: Small, poor and not worth much. ---
examples: He grew up in a one-horse town in Nebraska.
It's a one-horse operation — just him and a truck.
The place felt like a one-horse village after Chicago.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a one-horse town
entries.contrast: Nearly always in a one-horse town, meaning a tiny, dull place. The literal sense — a wagon pulled by one horse — is long gone from daily speech.

entries.meaning: Done, run or performed by a single person. ---
examples: The store is a one-man operation.
He put on a one-man show at the little theater downtown.
It was a one-man campaign against the new highway.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a one-man show
entries.contrast: One-woman and one-person work exactly the same way: a one-woman show, a one-person operation.

entries.meaning: Between just two people. ---
examples: I had a one-on-one meeting with my manager.
The tutoring is one-on-one.
He's better in one-on-one conversation than in a group.
entries.position: both
entries.contrast: Also an adverb and a noun: We met one-on-one, She asked for a one-on-one with the boss.

entries.meaning: Governed by a single political party, with no real opposition. ---
examples: It has been a one-party state for forty years.
One-party rule ended there in 1990.
The country held its first free vote after decades of one-party government.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: one-party rule

entries.meaning: Made in a single piece instead of separate parts. ---
examples: She bought a black one-piece swimsuit.
The baby was in a one-piece snowsuit.
The tub and surround come as a one-piece unit.
entries.position: attributive only — before a noun: a one-piece swimsuit
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the swimsuit itself: She wore a one-piece.

entries.meaning: One-sided has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The article gives a very one-sided account of the strike.
His version of the fight is one-sided.
The game was one-sided from the first quarter.
Their friendship is one-sided — she does all the calling.
It was the most one-sided election in years.

senses.head: Showing only one point of view; unfair
examples: The article gives a very one-sided account of the strike.
His version of the fight is one-sided.

senses.head: So unequal that one side does all the work or all the winning
examples: The game was one-sided from the first quarter.
Their friendship is one-sided — she does all the calling.
It was the most one-sided election in years.

entries.position: both

entries.meaning: One-time has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The gym charges a one-time signup fee of fifty dollars.
This is a one-time offer, so don't wait.
Congress approved a one-time payment to every household.
The one-time mayor now runs a bakery downtown.
Her one-time partner testified against her.

senses.head: Happening only once, not repeated
examples: The gym charges a one-time signup fee of fifty dollars.
This is a one-time offer, so don't wait.
Congress approved a one-time payment to every household.

senses.head: Former; in that job or role before
examples: The one-time mayor now runs a bakery downtown.
Her one-time partner testified against her.

entries.position: attributive only — a one-time fee, never the fee is one-time
entries.contrast: For 'former', American writing usually drops the hyphen: a onetime champion. For 'happening once', keep it: a one-time payment.

entries.meaning: One-to-one has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Every student gets an hour of one-to-one tutoring a week.
He asked for a one-to-one meeting with the director.
The coaching is one-to-one, not in groups.
There is a one-to-one match between the codes and the files.
The translation is not one-to-one, since one Russian word can cover three English ones.

senses.head: Between two people only, with no one else involved
examples: Every student gets an hour of one-to-one tutoring a week.
He asked for a one-to-one meeting with the director.
The coaching is one-to-one, not in groups.

senses.head: Matching one item to exactly one other item
examples: There is a one-to-one match between the codes and the files.
The translation is not one-to-one, since one Russian word can cover three English ones.

entries.русский: индивидуальный, один на один; взаимно однозначный
entries.position: both — one-to-one tutoring; the sessions are one-to-one
entries.contrast: Americans also say one-on-one for the teaching and meeting sense: a one-on-one meeting. One-to-one is the usual form for matching numbers.

entries.meaning: Done or performed by a single woman. ---
examples: She took her one-woman show to three cities.
The bakery is basically a one-woman operation.
It was a one-woman campaign against the new highway.
entries.position: attributive only
entries.form: compound — one + woman; the noun stays singular: a one-woman show
entries.contrast: A one-woman band keeps the singular woman, never women. The male form is one-man.

entries.meaning: Needing a lot of effort and feeling like a burden. ---
examples: The new paperwork is onerous for small businesses.
He called the contract terms onerous and walked away.
